Partial Demolition

Taking part of it down, and protecting what stays

Removing part of a structure while the rest remains: extensions, garages, sheds, carports, verandahs and pools. The work is defined by what stays rather than by what goes, which is why it is a different job from a knockdown even when it looks smaller.

0456 220 552

Carried out under demolition licence AD214737

Before anything starts

Six things have to be settled first, and not all of them are ours

Most jobs that run late run late on this list rather than on the work itself. Each line says who owns it.

  1. 01

    Hazardous materials survey of the part coming out

    Who Max, through an accredited laboratory

    An extension added in the 1970s often carries more asbestos than the original house does.

  2. 02

    Structural advice on what is being removed

    Who You, through an engineer

    Whether the part coming out is doing any work for the part that stays. This is the one that cannot be assumed.

  3. 03

    Approval or exemption

    Who You or your certifier

    Some partial demolition is exempt development and some is not. Which one it is depends on the property, not on the size of the job.

  4. 04

    Service isolation to the removed section

    Who You, with each authority

    Power, water and gas to the part coming out, isolated without cutting the part that stays.

  5. 05

    Make good scope

    Who Agreed between you and us before we start

    What the exposed face looks like when we leave: capped, sealed, weatherproofed, or left for your builder.

  6. 06

    Protection of the retained structure

    Who Max

    Bracing, propping and weather protection, designed around what the engineer says is needed.

The detail

What makes partial work harder than a knockdown

  • The cut line is the job. Everything is decided by where the new edge is and what condition it has to be in when we leave.
  • What stays has to be held up. If the removed section is doing structural work, propping and bracing go in before anything comes out, to a design rather than to a guess.
  • There is no room for the machine to swing. Close to a retained wall, much of the work is done by hand or with a small machine, which costs hours rather than horsepower.
  • The weather does not wait. An opened wall or roof needs protecting the same day. That is planned, not improvised.
  • The asbestos is often in the part coming out. Later additions carry fibro, eaves and wet area linings, and they have to be removed under clearance before the structure does.
  • The retained face is somebody else’s next job. Agreeing what condition it is handed over in, before we start, is what stops the argument at the end.

Where the machine cannot go, the work goes by hand

Before you book

What people ask about this one

Do I need approval to remove an extension?
Sometimes. Some partial demolition is exempt development and some needs consent, and which one applies depends on the property, the zoning and whether anything is heritage affected. Your certifier answers that, not us, and it is worth asking before you book anything.
Will the rest of the house be safe?
That is what the propping and bracing are for, and what the engineer’s advice decides. If the section coming out is carrying load, the support goes in first. We will not take a wall out and work out afterwards what it was holding.
What condition is the exposed face left in?
Whatever is agreed before we start. Capped and weather protected is the usual demolition scope; rendering, cladding and flashing it permanently is builder work. Putting that in writing beforehand is the single best thing you can do on a partial job.
Can you take out a pool?
Yes, and it is as much an excavation job as a demolition one. The shell comes out, the hole is backfilled in layers and compacted, because a pool void that was simply filled is where a future slab finds a soft spot.
Is partial demolition cheaper than a knockdown?
Per square metre, usually not. There is less material but far more care, more hand work and more protection. What it saves is the rest of the building.

Show us the line and what has to stay

A photograph with the section marked on it, and a word about what your builder needs the exposed face to look like. That is most of a partial demolition scope.

  • Propping and bracing to the engineer’s advice, not to a guess
